episodes.214544: Higher surface moisture was in place across central and eastern NM on August 1st behind a backdoor front with upper level high pressure over Arizona and Utah. Daytime heating resulted in the development of thunderstorms across the higher terrain midday. One storm became severe near Mora and produced half dollar to ping pong ball size hail in town as well as flash flooding damage on Highway 94 from Mora, NM to the Mora and San Miguel County line. Storms moved south and southeast and coalesced into a broken line across the highlands of central New Mexico and the eastern plains during the afternoon and early evening hours resulting in severe thunderstorm wind gusts at several sites across White Sands Missile Range and localized flash flooding near Capitan. Storms tapered off across southern New Mexico during the late evening hours.
episodes.214589: Drier air wrapped around the upper high circulation centered over the Four Corners into much of northern and central New Mexico on August 2nd. Higher moisture lingered across southwest New Mexico resulting in thunderstorm development across the Gila Mountains during the afternoon hours. Storms over the Sacaton burn scar southeast of Mogollon resulted in burn scar flash flooding on and downstream of the burn scar impacting the Willow Creek Subdivision. Storms across the Gila Mountains tapered off during the evening with the loss of daytime heating.

episodes.214624: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed in a humid airmass ahead of an approaching cold front, producing flash flooding across portions of Union, Lycoming and Sullivan counties. A separate line of storms produced localized flash flooding near Boswell in Somerset County and in Bedford County.
episodes.214743: Widely scattered thunderstorms resulted in gale-force winds in the waters around central to southern Maryland.
episodes.214761: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across central GA, associated with a shortwave trough, in an unstable environment (>2000 MLCAPE) and lifted northeastward into the CSRA and Midlands of SC.
episodes.214762: Scattered convection developed within an weak to moderately unstable environment during the afternoon on 8/1. Strong west to east moisture advection occurred with PWATs rising from around 1.5-1.7 inches in the morning to around 2.3-2.5 inches by early evening. A stalled frontal boundary provided a focus for low level convergence and nearly parallel mid level flow to the boundary orientation allowed  for training storms resulting in urban flash flooding.

episodes.215384: Thunderstorms developed in a very unstable atmosphere. There was enough flow for storms to be moving, but some storms trained over one another, resulting in several instances of flash flooding. Localized rainfall amounts of two to four inches were observed.
episodes.215862: August started off on an active note, with several rounds of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area. This stemmed from a low pressure system that ushered a warm front into West Virginia on August 2nd, maintaining a warm and unsettled environment for storms to thrive. The bulk of activity wound down during the evening, however some additional storms accompanied a cold front that swept through the area that night. The front stalled just east of the Appalachian Mountains on the 3rd, allowing isolated to scattered showers to linger over eastern West Virginia for much of the day. ||Storms featured during this timeframe were strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts that brought down trees and power lines. Storm damage was mainly observed in the foothills of the state, including Braxton, Clay, Webster, and Fayette Counties. A good portion of West Virginia received around an inch of rain, with pockets of two to three inch accumulations in central and southeast parts of the state. The highest 72-hour rainfall amounts, ranging from three to four inches, accrued in eastern Raleigh and Fayette Counties. This led to flooding on several roads.
episodes.216132: A decaying cluster of storms moved into Eddy and Lea counties overnight on August 1st. These storms had produced a strong outflow boundary which had begun to outrun convection. A 59 mph wind gust was recorded at the Artesia AWOS as the outflow boundary moved through.
episodes.216530: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced several wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.217010: Slow moving thunderstorms dumped heavy rainfall across Bay county and resulted in flash flooding.  In addition, scattered afternoon and evening thunderstorms produced sporadic wind damage across the area.
episodes.217352: On the afternoon of August 2nd, 2026, the eastern shores of Ohio and western shores of Pennsylvania were situated underneath a stationary boundary. This boundary would slowly move east across the lake developing showers as it moved and several waterspouts formed as a result of the updrafts from these showers. Across that portion of the lake, there was a plume of around 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear.
episodes.217371: Scattered storms developed across portions of eastern Virginia on August 2. While these storms were not severe, cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were present and resulted in the fatality of livestock.
episodes.217372: Scattered storms moves across the Chesapeake bay on August 2, producing gusty winds.
episodes.217445: Rounds of thunderstorms associated with a prefrontal trough and surface cold front crossed the region on August 2nd. Isolated instances of damaging wind gusts were observed from small-scale bowing structures. Also, training and back-building showers and thunderstorms create isolated flooding across the region. Rainfall rates ranged from 2 to 4 inches per hour in some areas.
episodes.217684: An upper level trough dug into the Lower Mississippi Valley on August 1st and 2nd.  An attendant cold front was positioned along the I-10 corridor the morning of August 2nd as the front gradually shifted southward through the area.  A persistent band of back-building thunderstorms developed ahead of the front over Assumption Parish and produced very heavy rainfall resulting in flash flooding of area roadways and yards.
episodes.217706: A stalled frontal boundary to the northwest of the region, combined with the usual late summer daytime heating/influences of sea breezes, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the area. Precipitable Water (PWAT) values reached as high as 2.2 to 2.5 inches during this period, which strongly supported heavy rain and flooding potential.
episodes.217721: An upper level trough dug into the Lower Mississippi Valley on August 1st and 2nd. An attendant cold front was positioned along the I-10 corridor the morning of August 2nd as the front gradually shifted southward through the area. A line of thunderstorms producing strong marine thunderstorm wind gusts developed ahead of the front and swept across the New Orleans region, including Lake Borgne in the morning hours of August 2nd.
episodes.217898: Southeast low level flow brought in good low level moisture to southern New Mexico with increasing northerly flow aloft. An upper level disturbance triggered thunderstorms over the higher terrain with training storms resulting in flash flooding in Otero and Grant counties.  A dust storm and large hail were also reported in southwest New Mexico.
episodes.217902: A weak cold front generated showers and thunderstorms across South-Central Texas. Some of these storms produced heavy rain leading to minor flooding.
episodes.217930: Shortwave energy approaching from the northeast Gulf encountered deep moisture and modest instability, helping produce deep convection capable of strong wind gusts across coastal waters.
episodes.218092: Training and back-building showers and thunderstorms created flooding ahead of a passing front. Rainfall rates ranged from 2-4 inches per hour.
episodes.218108: A cluster of strong thunderstorms moved southward along the Middle Texas Coast during the early morning hours on August 2nd. Strong downbursts brought winds of 39 to 44 mph along the bays, islands, and nearshore water of the Middle Texas Coast.
episodes.218147: On August 2nd, 2026, the Weather Prediction Center placed Western New York under a Marginal Excessive Rainfall Outlook as a tropical-moisture-rich environment interacted with an incoming slow-moving boundary. Area Forecast Discussions from NWS Buffalo emphasized unseasonably high precipitable water values, warning that repeated rounds of heavy showers and thunderstorms could produce intense rainfall rates exceeding two inches per hour. A widespread Flood Watch was hoisted across all of Western New York, and multiple Flash Flood Warnings were subsequently issued by late afternoon and evening as convective storms trained across the region, including north-central Erie County. The resulting downpours led to rapid urban runoff, road inundations, and localized flash flooding across vulnerable low-lying infrastructure throughout the metro area.
episodes.218150: On August 2nd, 2026, the Storm Prediction Center outlined portions of Western and Central New York under a Marginal convective risk as a slow-moving frontal boundary tapped into an unstable, tropical-moisture-laden environment. Area Forecast Discussions from NWS Buffalo highlighted that daytime surface heating interacting with high dew points created moderate CAPE, though overall severe potential remained closely tied to localized boundaries. Convection crossing over from Southern Ontario intensified along the Niagara Frontier during the early afternoon, prompting NWS Buffalo to issue a brief Tornado Warning for western Niagara County as radar indicated low-level rotation. As storm clusters tracked through the county, they produced isolated straight-line wind damage���including a downed utility pole near Youngstown���alongside torrential downpours.

Area Forecast Discussions from NWS Buffalo highlighted that daytime surface heating interacting with high dew points created moderate CAPE, though overall severe potential remained closely tied to localized boundaries. Convection crossing over from Southern Ontario intensified along the Niagara Frontier during the early afternoon, prompting NWS Buffalo to issue a brief Tornado Warning for western Niagara County as radar indicated low-level rotation. As storm clusters tracked through the county, they produced isolated straight-line wind damage���including a downed utility pole near Youngstown���alongside torrential downpours.
episodes.218205: Moderately strong instability coupled with weak shear produced isolated strong to severe thunderstorms in primarily southeastern Tennessee. A weak tornado was produced by a supercell thunderstorm in far northern Bledsoe County. This is the 8th recorded tornado to occur in the month of August in NWS Morristown's database. Additionally, heavy rainfall from storms later in the evening led to significant flash flooding near the towns of Ducktown and Copperhill.
episodes.218345: A cluster of thunderstorms moved across northeast Georgia during mid-afternoon. A couple of isolated embedded storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.218346: A cluster of thunderstorms moved east across Spartanburg County during late afternoon. The storms produced a brief, small, but fairly intense area of damaging wind gusts on the west side of the Spartanburg metro area.
episodes.218387: A dissipating cold front moved into south Texas during the afternoon of August 2nd, aided by a weak upper level disturbance moving into the same region.  Abundant moisture ahead of the front and lift from the disturbance triggered clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms in Brooks, western Hidalgo, and eastern Starr County - the only significant rain event of the month for the region.  Measured and estimated rainfall of 3 to 5 inches fell in southwest Brooks, with 2-3 inches elsewhere in the affected area.||The storms produced minor flooding in the City of McAllen, along with localized severe thunderstorm wind gusts.

The first damage was observed southwest of Franklin, where several large tree limbs were downed along Hamilton-Middletown Road and State Route 73. As the tornado moved northeast, more tree damage was noted on Dayton-Oxford Road, and a section of a corn field near Water Source Drive was flattened. Just northeast of Water Source Drive, one large metal building at an industrial facility had a large portion of a northwest-facing wall removed, along with a portion of the roof. Damage at this location supported wind speed estimates of 80 mph.||Several tree limbs were downed in a neighborhood near Forest Ave, Chestnut Street, and Park Ave. One house on Park Ave had some siding damage. The tornado first developed near Stacy Road, where corn field damage was evident on satellite imagery. The tornado then moved north, toward Germantown Liberty Road, south of Forney Road, where additional corn field damage and some tree damage were observed. The tornado then moved due north, on a track that closely approximated Snyder Road until reaching U.S. Route 35. Along this stretch of Snyder Road, there was extensive tree damage, including a few large trees uprooted or broken near the base. One barn on the east side of Snyder Road lost a portion of its roof.||North of U.S. Route 35, some shingle damage occurred at a business, with a few garage doors damaged at a storage facility. Some additional tree damage was noted to the north of these businesses. Satellite imagery depicted additional corn damage as the tornado progressed to the north. The tornado dissipated just east of Snyder Road, near Old Dayton Road.
